source.title_on_document: 생성형 AI 활용이 대학생의 창의적 아이디어 생성에 미치는 영향: 동일 과제 반복 수행에서의 사용 전환 효과 / The Effects of Generative AI Use on University Students’ Creative Idea Generation: Switching Effects in Repeated Task Performance

paper_design_summary: Students taking IT-related courses at two Korean universities (164 analyzed) did the task 'Imagining an Idea That Will Change the Future in 2035' twice in one session: in round 1 (10 minutes, up to 10 ideas) group A could use generative AI (ChatGPT free plan by default, 83 analyzed) and group B could not (81 analyzed), and the paper does not say how A and B were formed. After a break of about 30 minutes with a YouTube video, each group was split at random for a 10-minute round 2 that upgraded the round-1 ideas: A kept AI (A1, 43 analyzed) or lost it (A2, 40), and B adopted AI (B1, 41) or stayed without it (B2, 40). Two raters blind to condition scored every idea on a four-dimension rubric (novelty, usefulness/feasibility, elaboration/specificity, future-change fit), summed to a 0-100 total per participant per round.

studies.label: Classroom experiment: round-2 AI switching randomized within each round-1 group (2035 future-ideas task)

assignment.what_was_assigned: The round-2 AI condition, assigned at random within each round-1 group: in A (AI in round 1), keep AI (A1) or stop AI (A2); in B (no AI in round 1), adopt AI (B1) or continue without AI (B2). The paper does not say how students were placed in round-1 groups A and B and never calls that split random; all three randomization statements (PDF pp. 2, 5, 8) describe the round-2 split. Comparisons that cross the A/B split are coded in S2.

task.description: 'Imagining an Idea That Will Change the Future in 2035': propose ideas in any form (software, product, service, policy) that could improve life under future social changes (climate change, aging, urban crowding, mental health, changing relationships); up to 10 ideas per round. Round 1: produce as many diverse ideas as possible. Round 2: upgrade the round-1 output by revising, supplementing, or elaborating ideas or adding new perspectives.
task.duration: Round 1: 10 minutes; a break of about 30 minutes with an unrelated YouTube video; round 2: 10 minutes; one session

outcomes.name: Round-1-to-round-2 gain in total creativity score, with vs without AI in the round-2 upgrade (mixed-model planned contrasts H3 and H4)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two independent raters blind to condition scored each idea on four dimensions (novelty, usefulness/feasibility, elaboration/specificity, future-change fit), summed to a 0-10 idea score, with 1-3 point novelty deductions for similar or duplicate ideas within a round; participant total = sum of up to 10 idea scores (0-100), averaged over the two raters. The total mixes quantity and quality (mean ideas 9.18 in round 1, 9.52 in round 2). The paper does not say who the raters were, so the code human_raters is provisional (open question 3). Before scoring, the raters agreed on how to apply the rubric, the judgment rules for each dimension, and the deduction rule for similar ideas, and then each scored independently. ICC for the total, single/average: round 1 .918/.957, round 2 .920/.958; dimension ICCs over all 328 outputs: novelty .921, usefulness/feasibility .929, elaboration/specificity .912, future-change fit .848. Analysis: linear mixed model score ~ time x group_2 + (1 | person), reference group A1; the paper reports the time x group_2 planned contrasts as its main analysis. Gain = round 2 minus round 1. Within each contrast both arms produced round 1 under the same AI condition (none for B1 and B2, AI for A1 and A2), so the arms differ only in AI access during round 2. The two contrasts use disjoint subsamples randomized separately (B: 81 people analyzed; A: 83 analyzed). Within-arm paired t-tests of the gain (Table 3) are interpretive aids. Dimension-level results by arm are not reported.
outcomes.delay: Round 2 about 30 minutes after round 1, same session

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Within round-1 group B, students were randomly assigned to adopt AI for the round-2 upgrade (B1, 41 analyzed) or to continue without AI (B2, 40 analyzed), and within group A to keep AI (A1, 43 analyzed) or stop it (A2, 40 analyzed) (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, step 3; PDF p. 8, Section 5.1). S1 analyzes 164 people, and each randomized stratum alone has more than 50 (B 81, A 83). Two raters blind to condition scored every idea on a creativity rubric (PDF p. 6, Section 3.2.4; Table 4, PDF p. 7). The numbers assigned and dropped are not stated, and only students who wrote both outputs were analyzed. S2 holds the round-1 A vs B comparison (H1) and the A2 vs B2 comparison for the same 164 students. The paper never says how students entered A or B, so S2 is coded design_class other, and criterion 1 is unclear for S2. The paper's core status rests on S1 and does not depend on S2.

one_line_finding: Students randomly given AI for the round-2 upgrade raised their 0-100 rubric creativity score by 28.63 points more than students kept without AI (SE 2.49, 95% CI [23.74, 33.52]; gains 37.73 vs 9.10), and students randomly cut off from AI gained 5.50 points less than those who kept it (SE 2.47, p = .026) (PDF pp. 7-8, Section 4.4.2; Table 4).
open_questions: How were students placed in round-1 groups A (AI) and B (no AI)? The paper states randomization only for the round-2 split within A and within B, so H1 (S2-O1, d = 2.08) and the A2 vs B2 comparison (S2-O2) are not shown to be randomized, and S2 is coded design_class other. If the authors confirm random assignment, S2 becomes a field_rct with randomized contrasts. If the split was not random, S2 is observational context.
How many students began the task, and how many were dropped for not completing both rounds?
Rater background (lay or expert) is not stated ('2명의 독립 평가자'); coded human_raters as a provisional code, could be expert_raters.
Design class of S1: one supervised session inside IT-related courses that the paper calls an educational field experiment in an actual class context; coded field_rct, could be read as lab_rct.
The total score sums up to 10 idea scores, so it mixes quantity and quality; the paper says it cannot fully separate them (PDF p. 5, Section 3.2.2; PDF p. 9, Section 5.2).
notes: Locators give the PDF page (1-10) and the journal page (40-49); journal page = PDF page + 39. No diversity or similarity outcome is measured, and idea counts are reported only for the whole sample (9.18 and 9.52), so there is no fluency outcome by arm. Other printed results not coded as contrasts: H2, the pooled within-person change from round 1 46.57 (SD 23.19) to round 2 60.93 (SD 19.66), paired t(163) = 10.34, p < .001, mean change 14.36, 95% CI [11.62, 17.10], dz = 0.81 (Table 2 and Section 4.3, PDF p. 7), a repetition effect with no AI contrast; H5, the asymmetry (B1 - B2) - (A1 - A2) = 23.13, SE = 3.51, z = 6.60, p < .001, 95% CI [16.26, 30.00] (PDF p. 8, Section 4.4.2 item 3), a difference of the two coded contrasts. B1 vs B2 is the cleanest randomized AI-vs-no-AI estimate; B1's round-2 output is an AI-assisted upgrade of an unassisted draft. A1 vs A2 is coded with_ai because A1 had AI when its round-2 output was produced; the comparison of unassisted output after AI use is S2-O2. S1 and S2 are one sample, the same 164 students: S2 holds only the comparisons that cross the round-1 A/B split, whose allocation the paper does not state. The mixed-model SEs come from participant-round scores with a random intercept per person. The paper reports written consent but no ethics-board approval, preregistration, funding statement, or data link. company_involvement is true only because of the first author's bank employment; no company had a stated role in the study. Finalized 2026-10-05: the four challenge problems (two from the assignment lens, one from the outcome lens, one from the people lens) were checked against the PDF. Three were corrected. The round-1 A vs B contrast (the reconciliation's final S1-O2, now S2-O1) and the A2 vs B2 contrast (final S1-O3, now S2-O2) moved from the randomized study S1 to a new study S2 with design_class other and randomized not_stated, the coding that c054, c094, and c168 use for an unstated allocation. participants.who now says year and major were not systematically collected. One problem stays open: the rater code human_raters, now marked provisional. Spec alignment: counts in paper_design_summary, eligibility.reason, and S1-O1's measure_detail now say 'analyzed', and participants.exclusions says the completers rule can drop people after the round-2 draw. Other edits: the break is 'about 30 minutes' (약 30분, PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, step 2), and source.version says the captions are in English only. The reconciliation object is unchanged, so it still records six arms in S1 and the ids S1-O2 and S1-O3 for the two contrasts that the final form moves to S2.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1-O2 (H1, round-1 A vs B, d = 2.08) sat in study S1, coded field_rct and randomized yes, although the paper never says how students entered groups A and B. Only the prose in measure_detail said that the contrast is not shown to be randomized.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: The study is split. H1 moved from S1-O2 to S2-O1 in a new study S2 for the same 164 students, coded design_class other with assignment.randomized not_stated, unit other, structure between, and arms A, B, A2, and B2. S1 keeps the randomized round-2 contrasts (S1-O1) and the arms A1, A2, B1, and B2. The code other follows c054, c094, and c168 for an unstated allocation, because quasi_people would assert a non-random assignment that the paper does not state either. paper_design_summary, the S1 label, eligibility.reason, open_questions, and notes now say so. A search of the PDF text layer finds 무작위 only on PDF pp. 2, 5, and 8, each time for the round-2 split, and Figure 1 (5x render) has no allocation label.

open_items.item: Round-1 allocation (open question 1): how students entered groups A and B. The paper states randomization only for the round-2 split, so S2 (H1 and A2 vs B2) is coded design_class other with criterion 1 unclear for S2. The paper's core status rests on S1 and does not change. The paper mentions no supplement, preregistration, or posted data, so only the authors can settle it.
open_items.scope_note: Affects S2 only; the randomized round-2 comparisons in S1 establish paper-level eligibility (final.core yes).

open_items.item: Students who started, were assigned, and were dropped (open question 2). Criterion 2 rests on the 164 people analyzed in S1 (81 and 83 in the two randomized strata), and a count at assignment can only be larger.

Rater background (open question 3): human_raters is provisional, and expert_raters applies if the two raters were domain experts or instructors. Criterion 3 accepts scoring by raters of any background.

Design class of S1 (open question 4): field_rct (the paper's educational field experiment in an actual class context) or lab_rct (one supervised session). Both are randomized codes, so criterion 1 holds either way.

Quantity and quality in the total (open question 5): the score sums up to 10 idea scores, and the paper prints no idea counts or per-idea mean scores by arm. Criterion 3 holds either way, because the raters scored each idea.

audit_corrections.basis: Affects S2 only; the randomized round-2 comparisons in S1 establish paper-level eligibility (final.core yes).
